topic: Criminal Law: Comparative Analysis and Transitional Provisions
description: This module focuses on the transition from the old criminal justice system (IPC, CrPC, IEA) to the new regime (BNS, BNSS, BSA) which came into effect on July 1, 2024. It covers the 'Repeal and Savings' clauses, the constitutional bar on retrospective criminal laws, and how pending cases, investigations, and new FIRs for old offenses are handled during this transition.

constitutional_framework_retrospectivity.concept: Constitutional Framework: Protection Against Retrospective Laws
key_points: Article 20(1): The Constitution of India strictly prohibits 'ex post facto' (retroactive) substantive criminal laws. A person cannot be convicted for an act that was not an offense at the time of its commission, nor can they be subjected to a penalty greater than what existed then.

Substantive vs. Procedural: While substantive laws (like BNS creating new offenses) cannot apply retrospectively to acts committed before their enactment, procedural laws (like BNSS and BSA) generally can apply retrospectively to pending cases, UNLESS the new statute explicitly includes a 'savings clause' stating otherwise.

repeal_and_savings_clauses.concept: Repeal and Savings Clauses (Sec 358 BNS, Sec 531 BNSS, Sec 170 BSA)
key_points: Purpose: The new laws explicitly repeal the IPC, CrPC, and IEA. However, they include 'Savings' clauses to prevent a legal vacuum and ensure continuity of justice for past acts.

Pending Proceedings (Section 531 BNSS): The BNSS explicitly states that any appeal, application, trial, inquiry, or investigation pending immediately before July 1, 2024, shall be disposed of, continued, or held in accordance with the provisions of the old CrPC, as if the new BNSS had not come into force.

Protection of Past Liabilities: Any right, privilege, obligation, or liability incurred under the old laws (IPC) remains fully intact. Punishments incurred under the IPC for crimes committed before July 1, 2024, will be carried out under the IPC framework.

comparative_analysis_application.concept: Comparative Analysis: Determining the Applicable Law in Practice
key_points: Offenses Before July 1, 2024 (Pending Cases): If an FIR was already registered and investigation/trial was ongoing before July 1, 2024, the entire matter is governed by IPC, CrPC, and IEA.
Offenses After July 1, 2024: For any crime committed on or after this date, the new regime (BNS, BNSS, BSA) applies completely.

The Hybrid Scenario (Old Crime, New FIR): If a crime was committed in 2023, but the victim registers the FIR on August 10, 2024, the substantive law applied will be the IPC (due to Article 20(1)). However, the procedure for investigation, arrest, and trial will be governed by the new BNSS.

questions.question: Which Article of the Indian Constitution strictly prohibits the retrospective application of new substantive criminal laws (ex post facto laws), ensuring a person is only punished under the law in force at the time the act was committed?
questions.explanation: Article 20(1) grants protection against ex post facto laws. It ensures that the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) cannot be used to penalize someone for an act committed before it came into force on July 1, 2024, if that act was not a crime under the IPC.

questions.question: A criminal trial for theft (under the old IPC and CrPC) started in January 2024 and is still ongoing in August 2024. According to the 'Savings Clause' in Section 531 of the BNSS, which procedural law will govern the remainder of this trial?

options.A: The trial must be restarted entirely under the new BNSS.
options.B: The trial will continue and be disposed of under the provisions of the old CrPC, 1973.
options.C: The judge has the discretion to choose between CrPC and BNSS.
options.D: The case is automatically dismissed because the old laws have been repealed.

questions.explanation: Section 531 of the BNSS explicitly states that all appeals, applications, trials, inquiries, or investigations pending immediately before the commencement of the BNSS shall continue under the old CrPC as if the BNSS had never come into force.

questions.question: A person commits a fraud in December 2023. The victim discovers the fraud later and goes to the police station to file an FIR on August 15, 2024 (after the new laws came into force). Which combination of substantive and procedural laws will apply to this new FIR?
questions.explanation: Because the offense was committed before July 1, 2024, the substantive law applicable is the IPC (protection against retrospective criminal law). However, since the legal machinery (FIR/investigation) was initiated after July 1, 2024, the new procedural law (BNSS) will govern how the police and courts handle the case going forward.
